AI for Mobility · Section 4.14 · Reading library

How traffic flow theory gets into AI models

Thirty-eight papers from 2021 to 2026, read in full, and 64 more listed. They are sorted by the role traffic theory plays and where it plugs in: the training data, the model itself, the loss, the moment the model runs, or the check afterwards. Each card shows the paper’s key figure, the same five facts, and what the physics bought.

The mapThe papersWhat each way guaranteesHow the field movedCheck yourselfSources

Two questions place every paper

Ask of any paper: is the traffic theory still there when the finished model runs? And: where does it plug in? The first question splits the papers into the two big groups. The second gives the code on each card. This is the same idea as the four places in sections 4.11 and 4.12 of the course notes, widened from generative models to every kind of model.

Traffic theory can enter at five stations of an ordinary AI pipeline. Gold codes act only during training; green codes are still inside the model when it predicts or controls. The color of each card in this library follows the same key.

2aPhysics-shaped layersThe network's own layers are built like the physics: conservation as message passing, kernels limited to the wave speeds, outputs that cannot break a balance.54

1 · Theory guides training

The finished model is ordinary AI; the theory shaped it while it learned.

1a

Equation residual in the loss

The error of a traffic equation, computed on the network's own output, is added to the training loss. Where there is no data, the equation still has something to say, so the network can learn from a few detectors.

1a

PIDL+FDL2021

A Physics-Informed Deep Learning Paradigm for Traffic State and Fundamental Diagram Estimation

Shi et al. · IEEE T-ITS 2021 · paper ↗ · also 4 Learns the theory

Traffic task
Fill in the density (and speed) field of a freeway stretch from a few loop detectors, while also learning the fundamental diagram and the model parameters.
Physics used
The conservation law of LWR (with a small diffusion term ε in the synthetic test) or ARZ (with relaxation time τ). The FD is not assumed; a network learns it.
AI model
A fully connected network (8 hidden layers × 20 tanh nodes) maps (t, x) to density and speed. A second small network, the FD learner (2 × 20), maps density to flow or equilibrium speed.
Where the physics enters
In the loss. Automatic differentiation gives ρ_t and ρ_x; the LWR or ARZ residual, with the FD learner inside it, is squared at auxiliary points. The FD learner is trained only through this residual.
Data
Synthetic Greenshields LWR and ARZ ring roads (numerical solutions on a 960 × 240 grid) with 2–5 virtual loops; NGSIM US-101 averaged into 21 cells × 1,770 time steps, with 4–14 virtual loops.
Key lineloss = α·MSE(ρ̂ − ρ at loop detectors) + β·mean[(ρ̂_t + ∂ₓQ̂(ρ̂) − ε·ρ̂_xx)²] at auxiliary points, where Q̂ is the FD-learner network

A state network maps (t, x) to density; automatic differentiation gives its slopes. These go into the LWR (or ARZ) equation, whose flux term is not a Greenshields formula but a second small network, the FD learner. The squared equation error at auxiliary points (extra (t, x) points where only the equation is checked) is added to the loop-detector error. The state network, FD learner and parameters such as ε or τ are trained together, so the FD is found without flow observations. Idea to remember: keep the conservation law exact and let a network learn the part you trust least, the FD.

What they found
  • Synthetic LWR ring road (Table I): with three loop detectors, the diffusion coefficient learned inside the residual was 0.00495 against a true value of 0.005.
  • NGSIM US-101 (Fig. 7, conclusion): PIDL+FDL generally beat NN, LSTM, extended Kalman filter, interpolation, adaptive smoothing and PIDL with a fixed FD in accuracy and data efficiency; results are given only as a plot.
For mobility

An agency with sparse loop detectors could map density between them and get a site-specific fundamental diagram as a by-product, without assuming its shape in advance.

Watch out

Loss weights are grid-searched per site, the learned FD curled up at high density on NGSIM until a concavity penalty was added, and ARZ did worse than LWR.

1a

PIDL-CF2021

A Physics-Informed Deep Learning Paradigm for Car-Following Models

Mo, Shi & Di · Transportation Research Part C 2021 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Predict a following vehicle's acceleration at the next step from spacing, speed difference and its own speed; optionally calibrate the car-following model's parameters at the same time.
Physics used
IDM (v0, T0, s0, amax, b) and OVM (vmax, hc, k); GHR and FVDM tried on NGSIM. Parameters are calibrated first (least squares or genetic algorithm) or learned jointly.
AI model
A fully connected tanh network maps (spacing, Δv, v) to acceleration: 3 hidden layers of 60 units on simulated data, 5 larger layers on NGSIM. An LSTM version is also tested.
Where the physics enters
In the loss. At collocation states (sampled states with no observed acceleration) the network's acceleration must match the IDM/OVM acceleration; α weights this physics error against the data error.
Data
IDM- and OVM-simulated trajectories with Gaussian noise (four driving regimes for IDM); NGSIM US-101 (50 similar car-following cases, about 45K points) and NGSIM I-80.
Key lineloss = α · mean[(a_net − a_observed)²] + (1 − α) · mean[(a_net − a_IDM)²] at collocation states

The paper trains a neural car-following model with IDM (or OVM) as a second teacher. Observed state–action pairs give the usual data error. In addition, collocation states, extra (spacing, Δv, v) points with no observed acceleration, are fed to both the network and IDM, and the network is asked to agree with IDM there; the weight α trades the two errors. IDM is either calibrated first or its parameters sit inside the training graph and are learned with the network. Idea to remember: the best α is small when data are scarce and climbs toward 1 (pure data) as data grow.

What they found
  • Simulated IDM data (Fig. 8): on average, adding the IDM loss cut test MSE versus the same network without physics by 16.80% in emergency braking but only 1.26% in cruising.
  • NGSIM US-101 (Fig. 10): calibrated IDM and OVM used alone were the worst models, yet used as a physics loss they made the network beat its physics-free version.
For mobility

With few trajectories at a new site, an AV team or agency could train a learned following model that leans on IDM where data are thin.

Watch out

The gain shrinks as data grow and depends on the physics chosen: on NGSIM, OVM helped less than IDM, and the data-versus-physics weight α must be tuned.

1a

PRGP2021

Macroscopic Traffic Flow Modeling with Physics Regularized Gaussian Process: A New Insight into Machine Learning Applications in Transportation

Yuan, Zhang, Yang & Zhe · Transportation Research Part B 2021 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Estimate flow and speed at any (location, time) on a freeway stretch from four detectors, including when part of the training data is faulty.
Physics used
LWR conservation law, Payne–Whitham or ARZ (with momentum equations), written as stochastic equations Ψf = g; a heat equation serves as a deliberately wrong control.
AI model
A multi-output Gaussian process (GP: a probabilistic regression that returns a mean and an uncertainty) maps (x, t) to flow, density and speed, with SE-ARD and RBF kernels.
Where the physics enters
In the training objective. GP samples at 10 random points are pushed through the traffic equations; the residuals are scored by a zero-mean 'shadow GP' and added, with weight γ, to the data likelihood.
Data
Utah DOT PeMS data from four sensors on I-15, August 5–11, 2019, randomly split; a robustness test replaces 50% of training data with flows carrying 100 veh/5min noise.
Key lineobjective = log p(detector data | GP) + γ · E[log N(Ψf̂ ; 0, K̂)], with Ψf̂ = ∂ₜρ̂ + ∂ₓq̂ for LWR, evaluated on GP samples at random points Z

A Gaussian process (GP) returns a mean and an uncertainty for flow, density and speed at each (x, t). To add physics, the authors draw GP samples at random points, apply the LWR (or Payne–Whitham, ARZ) operator to them by automatic differentiation, and ask the resulting residuals to look like draws from a zero-mean 'shadow GP'. This term, weighted by γ, is added to the usual data likelihood, so physics acts as a soft penalty on the GP's answer rather than as part of its prior. Idea to remember: a residual penalty works for probabilistic models too, and helps most when the data are bad.

What they found
  • Flawed flows mixed into the training data (Table 3): the three PRGP models beat a pure GP by about 160 veh/h of RMSE and over 100% of MAPE in flow estimation.
  • Against the same traffic models calibrated alone (Table 2), the physics-regularized GPs were better by around 80 veh/5min in flow RMSE and 7 mph in speed RMSE.
For mobility

An agency whose detectors sometimes fail could use a traffic-flow-regularized estimator to keep flow and speed estimates reasonable when some readings are wrong.

Watch out

On clean data the gain over a plain GP was small, a wrong physics model (heat equation) made results worse, and GP cost grows with the cube of the sample size.

1a

TrafficFlowGAN2022

TrafficFlowGAN: Physics-informed Flow based Generative Adversarial Network for Uncertainty Quantification

Mo, Fu, Xu & Di · ECML PKDD 2022 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Estimate density and speed, with their spread, at every point of a freeway's space–time field from a few loop detectors: traffic state estimation with uncertainty.
Physics used
ARZ (conservation plus a momentum equation with relaxation τ) or LWR. The equilibrium speed Ueq(ρ) is a small network kept decreasing by a shape penalty; physics parameters are learned.
AI model
A conditional normalizing flow (a generator whose exact likelihood can be computed) turns noise and (x, t) into (ρ, u) samples; a CNN discriminator judges space–time patches.
Where the physics enters
In the generator loss: at unobserved (x, t) points the ARZ or LWR residual of generated samples, averaged over the noise, is squared and added to the other losses. The discriminator has no physics.
Data
A noisy ARZ ring-road solution (240 × 960 grid) seen by 4 sensors; NGSIM US-101 (15 minutes) with 3 to 18 virtual loop detectors.
Key linegenerator loss = α·(negative log-likelihood of detector data) + β·(adversarial loss) + γ·L_phy, with L_phy built from (E_z[ρ̂_t + (ρ̂û)_x])² and the ARZ momentum residual at unobserved (x, t)

TrafficFlowGAN outputs a spread of possible traffic states at each (x, t), not one value. A normalizing flow turns random noise plus (x, t) into a density and speed sample. It is trained to give the detector data high likelihood, to fool a CNN discriminator that looks at space–time patches, and to keep the ARZ or LWR residual small at unobserved points; the equilibrium-speed curve inside that residual is a small network learned along the way. Idea to remember: a PDE residual can regularize a generative model too, if you average it over the noise samples.

What they found
  • NGSIM US-101 (Fig. 7): the ARZ version had the lowest relative error for nearly all detector counts and the LWR version the lowest KL divergence, against a pure flow, physics-informed flows, a flow-GAN without physics and an ARZ-based EKF.
  • Training cost (Section 5.4): flow models with and without the physics loss both took 0.11 s per epoch, so computing the residual added almost no time.
For mobility

An agency could get uncertainty bands, not only point estimates, for speed and density between sparse detectors, and see where an estimate is too uncertain to act on.

Watch out

Results are shown only as plots for one 15-minute NGSIM segment, several loss weights need tuning, and the model must be retrained for each road or time slot.

1a

EGTML2024

An evolutionary game theory-based machine learning framework for predicting mandatory lane change decision

Xu et al. · Digital Transportation and Safety 2024 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Predict whether a driver who must leave the lane (US-101 lanes 5 and 6) changes lane now: yes or no, from 24 features of the driver and four surrounding vehicles.
Physics used
Two-player evolutionary game: lane changer (change or not) versus target-lane follower (yield or not). Payoffs use TTC, the follower's speed loss and distance to the lane-change end; replicator dynamics evolve both probabilities.
AI model
Four classifiers are tried: a neural network (ANN), random forest, LightGBM and XGBoost. LightGBM, a boosted-tree model, scored best (accuracy 0.865) and is the one used for all later results.
Where the physics enters
In the loss. The calibrated game labels traffic states with its own decision; loss = α·(disagreement with game) + (1 − α)·(disagreement with data), each measured with AUC. α = 0.1 worked best.
Data
NGSIM US-101 (Los Angeles, 640 m): 586 mandatory lane changes. A Gaussian mixture splits drivers into aggressive (616) and conservative (1,012), giving four driver-pair game types, each calibrated separately.
Key lineLoss = α · AUC_c (learner vs. game decisions) + (1 − α) · AUC_o (learner vs. observed decisions); game: dx/dt = x · (payoff of this choice − average payoff)

At a ramp or lane drop, the driver who must change lanes (SV) and the follower in the target lane (TB) play a game: SV changes or not, TB yields or not. Payoffs score safety (TTC), the follower's speed loss and the distance left to the lane-change area's end. Replicator dynamics let both choice probabilities evolve; the game predicts a change only if both exceed 0.5 and both TTCs pass a minimum. The calibrated game then labels the traffic states, and the classifier must agree with these labels and with the observed decisions. Idea to remember: any calibrated behavior model, even a game, can act as a second teacher.

What they found
  • Sensitivity test with EGT-LightGBM (Fig. 12a): the game-informed model beat plain LightGBM, especially with few training samples; the gap shrank as training data grew.
  • Lane-change positions for aggressive–aggressive driver pairs (Fig. 11a): KL divergence from the observed distribution was 0.231 for EGT-LightGBM versus 0.271 for plain LightGBM (lower is closer).
For mobility

An agency studying a work-zone lane drop or weaving section could train a lane-change predictor from few local trajectories by using a calibrated merging game as a second teacher.

Watch out

One NGSIM site, 586 lane changes; the gain shows mainly with few samples and only in plots, and the paper never explains how its AUC loss trains tree models.

1a

GenCast2026

Generalising Traffic Forecasting to Regions without Traffic Observations

Su et al. · AAAI 2026 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Forecast speeds 2 hours ahead, from the past 2 hours, at locations in a whole region with no sensors, using an adjacent region that has them.
Physics used
LWR conservation rewritten for speed with Greenshields: R = ∂x/∂t + (2x − x_free)·∂x/∂l. Free-flow speed per location = 85th-percentile off-peak speed.
AI model
A graph-convolution + temporal-convolution forecaster trained by hiding parts of the observed region (contrastive backbone from STSM), plus a weather cross-attention encoder and a spatial grouping module.
Where the physics enters
In the loss. Time and location get smooth embeddings (sinusoidal time; LLM- or GeoHash-based location), so autograd gives ∂/∂t and ∂/∂l of the forecast; the residual is penalized with a Huber loss.
Data
Speeds from PEMS-Bay, PEMS07, PEMS08, METR-LA (5-min) and Melbourne (15-min, urban), split in space 4:1:5 so test sensors form an unseen region; ERA5-Land weather.
Key lineloss = L_pred + λ·L_cl + µ·L_spg + θ·Huber(R), with R = ∂x̂/∂(time embedding) + (2x̂ − x_free)·∂x̂/∂(location embedding)

GenCast forecasts speeds for a region with no sensors by training on a neighbouring region where sensors are hidden on purpose. LWR needs density and a continuous road position, but the data are speeds on a sensor graph. So the authors use the Greenshields relation to write LWR in speed only, and give each time step and sensor a smooth embedding so automatic differentiation can take ∂/∂t and ∂/∂l of the forecast. The residual is penalized with a Huber loss (squared for small errors, linear for large ones). Idea to remember: a PDE loss on a sensor graph needs a differentiable stand-in for 'position along the road'.

What they found
  • Overall (Table 1): against the best competitor, usually STSM, GenCast cut forecast errors by up to 3.1% and raised R² by up to 125.6% (Melbourne) across five datasets.
  • Ablation (Fig. 3, Fig. 11): removing the LWR loss (w/o-phy) raised RMSE; the authors find it matters most for GenCast-L, whose LLM location embeddings are frozen, and for the dense Melbourne network.
For mobility

An agency with sensors in one district could forecast speeds in an adjacent district before installing detectors there, with LWR as a guide where no data exist.

Watch out

The space derivative is taken along a learned or LLM location embedding, not road distance; R² stays low and error gains over the best baseline are small (up to 3.1%).

1b

Rule or property in the loss

Instead of a full equation, the loss penalizes a broken rule: the sign of a response, string stability, or the shape of the fundamental diagram. In RL the reward plays the part of the loss, so a reward built from max-pressure or stability theory belongs here too.

1b

KIDL2025

A Knowledge-Informed Deep Learning Paradigm for Generalizable and Stability-Optimized Car-Following Models

Wang et al. · Communications in Transportation Research 2025 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Build a car-following model (speed, spacing, relative speed → acceleration) that works across freeway datasets and damps disturbances in a platoon.
Physics used
Local stability via monotonicity (fixed signs of ∂a/∂v, ∂a/∂s, ∂a/∂Δv) and the linear string-stability condition f_v² − 2f_s + 2f_v·f_Δv > 0 at equilibrium states.
AI model
An LLM (DeepSeek V2.5) labels 10,000 sampled scenarios, five answers each with a majority vote; a small neural network (the student) learns those labels.
Where the physics enters
In the student's loss. Autograd gives the slopes; wrong-signed spacing and relative-speed slopes are penalized at all samples, and the smallest string-stability value over grid-searched equilibria is pushed above zero.
Data
Scenarios sampled from truncated normal distributions fitted to NGSIM I-80, NGSIM US-101 and HighD; trajectories from these three datasets used for testing.
Key lineloss = MSE(a, LLM label) + θ_mon·C_mon + θ_str·max(0, −min over equilibria of [f_v² − 2f_s + 2f_v·f_Δv]), where f_v = ∂a/∂v, f_s = ∂a/∂s, f_Δv = ∂a/∂Δv

KIDL builds a car-following model in two steps. First, an LLM is asked to act as a driver: given speed, spacing and leader speed, it returns an acceleration. These answers become labels, and a small neural network learns to copy them. Second, because the student is a plain function of v, s and Δv, automatic differentiation (autograd) gives its slopes. The loss penalizes wrong-signed slopes (for local stability) and a negative value of the textbook string-stability test at equilibrium states (zero acceleration, zero relative speed) found by grid search. Idea to remember: classic stability conditions are written in partial derivatives, and a neural network gives you those derivatives for free.

What they found
  • Ablation on aggregated trajectory error across three datasets (Table 5): the monotonicity penalty cut error by 7.21% versus the unconstrained student, and the string-stability penalty cut it by a further 4.24%.
  • Weight sweep (Fig. 7): the lowest error came at a string-stability weight of 0.6, but that model was still string unstable; a weight of 0.9 made every equilibrium string stable (Fig. 8).
For mobility

An AV team could require a learned following controller to pass the same linear string-stability test used for IDM at every equilibrium, and train it to pass.

Watch out

Labels come from an LLM, not observed drivers, so LLM errors can carry over; stability is the linear test at grid-searched equilibria, and it trades off against accuracy.

1b

RACER2025

RACER: Rational Artificial Intelligence Car-following-model Enhanced by Reality

Li, Halatsis & Stern · IEEE T-ITS 2025 · paper ↗ · also 3 Tests the AI

Traffic task
Predict the next acceleration of an ACC car following a lead car, then run the model as a controller to rebuild the follower's speed and spacing.
Physics used
Rational driving constraints on signs only: ∂a/∂v ≤ 0, ∂a/∂s ≥ 0, ∂a/∂r ≥ 0 (v own speed, s spacing, r relative speed). OVRV is the physics baseline.
AI model
An LSTM reads the recent speed, spacing and relative speed; a dense branch reads the current state; the two merge to predict acceleration.
Where the physics enters
In the loss. Autograd gives the slope of predicted acceleration with respect to v, s and r; a ReLU keeps only wrong-signed slopes, which are added as penalties.
Data
Gunter et al. field tests of commercial ACC cars (10 Hz GPS, about 6000 rows); oscillatory trial, minimum- and maximum-gap settings; 80/10/10 split.
Key lineloss = MSE(a_pred, a_true) + λ1·mean[ReLU(∂a/∂v)] + λ2·mean[ReLU(−∂a/∂s)] + λ3·mean[ReLU(−∂a/∂r)]

RACER predicts an ACC car's acceleration from its recent speed, spacing and relative speed. During training, automatic differentiation (autograd) measures how the predicted acceleration changes when each input changes a little. A rational driver should not accelerate more when already faster, and should not brake harder when the gap grows or the leader pulls away. Any wrong-signed slope passes through a ReLU (keeps only positive values) and is added to the loss. No car-following equation is imposed, only the signs. The same sign test then checks a plain LSTM and an OVRV-based PINN. Idea to remember: you can teach a network the direction of a physical effect without picking one model.

What they found
  • Used as a controller at the maximum-gap ACC setting (Table 4), spacing RMSE was 0.394 m for RACER, 2.573 m for the OVRV-residual PINN and 22.761 m for OVRV; the plain LSTM caused a crash.
  • Sign check on minimum-gap test data (Fig. 7): the OVRV-residual PINN broke the speed and spacing rules about 50% of the time, while RACER had zero violations (Fig. 8).
For mobility

Before putting a learned car-following model into a microsimulator, screen it for wrong-signed responses to speed, gap and closing speed, and penalize them in training.

Watch out

The rule is a soft penalty with unreported weights, checked only at data points, on one set of controlled ACC tests; the authors call the errors best-case.

1b

MAML-MTPINN2026

Learning to Learn the Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram using Physics-Informed and Model Agnostic Machine Learning

Roark, Agriesti, Pereira & Cantelmo · Transportation Research Part C 2026 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Estimate a city's MFD (average flow versus average occupancy, critical occupancy, maximum flow) when only 10 to 75 loop detectors are available.
Physics used
Bi-parabolic MFD: a rising parabola through the origin and a falling parabola sharing a vertex at critical occupancy; congested branch 1–4 times as wide; no flow above the maximum.
AI model
MTPINN: shared fully connected layers with three heads (critical occupancy, maximum flow, average flow), meta-trained with MAML across cities so it adapts to a new city in 5 gradient steps.
Where the physics enters
In the loss: data MSE plus α times a shape term that pulls predicted flows toward two parabolas built from the network's own critical occupancy and maximum-flow outputs, plus three penalties.
Data
UTD19 loop-detector data, 20 cities with at least 100 detectors; subsets of 75, 50, 25 and 10 detectors sampled 30 times per city; Essen, Basel and Frankfurt as unseen cities.
Key lineL_total = L_MSE + α·L_Physics, with L_Physics = w1·L1 + w2·L2 + λ_offset + λ_scale + λ_max (L1, L2: misfit to the uncongested and congested parabolas)

Drawing a city's MFD needs many loop detectors, and many cities have few. The authors build a small network with three outputs: average flow at each occupancy, critical occupancy and maximum flow. The loss adds a shape term: the network's own critical occupancy and maximum flow define two parabolas meeting at one vertex, and predicted flows are pulled toward them. Penalties keep the congested parabola 1 to 4 times wider and stop flows above the maximum. Meta-learning (MAML: learning a starting point that adapts fast to a new task) is then run across cities. Idea to remember: a known curve shape can act as a soft guide when detector data are thin.

What they found
  • With only 10 detectors (Table 7), the meta-trained MTPINN had 17% lower MSE than the same meta-trained network without the physics loss (MAML-NN).
  • With 75 detectors (Table 5), mean flow MAE across cities was 30.34 with meta-learning versus 60.34 for MTPINN trained only on the target city's sampled data.
For mobility

A city with few loop detectors could reuse weights learned from detector-rich cities to sketch its MFD for perimeter control or congestion monitoring.

The shape loss alone gives high bias, at 25 and 50 detectors a plain network with meta-learning scored lower MSE (Tables 7–8), and the congested branch is barely observed.

MFDRLPC2021

Zhou & Gayah · Transportation Research Part C 2021 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Set two perimeter gating rates (between 0.1 and 0.9) every 60 s between a city center and its periphery to maximize trips completed in a 1-hour morning peak.
Physics used
Two-region MFD accumulation dynamics (vehicle conservation by region and destination); Yokohama MFD for the periphery, halved for the center (critical accumulations 8241 and 4120 veh).
AI model
Double DQN with Ape-X (many actors explore copies of the simulator, one learner updates the network); state = accumulations, expected demands and last controls; 9 actions.
Where the physics enters
Only as the training environment: the MFD model, with demand noise and MFD errors added, moves the system forward and returns the reward (trips completed). The agent never sees the MFD equations.
Data
No field data. Numerical two-region MFD simulation with Gaussian demand noise and MFD errors; five agents trained, then tested on 343 unseen settings of initial accumulation, demand and MFD error.
Key linedn₁₂/dt = q₁₂ − u₁₂·M₁₂, with M_ij = (n_ij / n_i)·f_i(n_i); reward = (M₁₁ + M₂₂) / C

Classic perimeter control, such as model predictive control (MPC), needs the MFD inside the controller. Here the MFD model only builds a practice world: the two-region MFD equations, with random demand noise and MFD errors, simulate how vehicle accumulations change in each 60-second step. A deep Q-network (a network that scores each possible action) tries raising, holding or lowering each gate, receives the trips completed as its reward, and learns which action pays off in each state. At run time the agent needs only current accumulations and demand estimates. Idea to remember: a traffic model can be the training ground for a controller even if the controller never reads its equations.

What they found
  • Unseen initial accumulations (Fig. 6): agents 1, 2, 3 and 5 beat MPC whenever the initial-accumulation increase φ was 0.15 or more, although MPC had full knowledge of the environment.
  • Unseen MFD errors (Fig. 8): MPC did best at most error levels, and when the true MFD was much higher than assumed (φ ≥ 0.4) both MPC and the agents did worse than no control.
For mobility

A city could train a gating controller offline on a calibrated two-region MFD model with noise, then deploy it without needing an exact MFD at run time.

Watch out

Training and testing both use the two-region MFD simulator, so effects it leaves out (uneven congestion inside a region, hysteresis, real signals) are untested.

Traffic task
Coordinate on-ramp metering and urban perimeter gating every 30 s across a network to minimize total travel time in a 3-hour morning peak.

Asymmetric CTM for freeways and ramps; generalized bathtub model with an Underwood-type MFD for urban regions; ALINEA (occupancy feedback) and Gating (MFD-based feedback) as teacher controllers.
AI model
One deep Q-network per ramp or perimeter: an MLP encoder plus an LSTM read local observations and score three actions (raise, hold or lower the rate by 0.05).

Data: the CTM-bathtub simulator is the training environment and gives the reward (trips completed). Loss: a demonstration term pulls each agent toward ALINEA or Gating actions; its weight fades to zero.

Small synthetic network (one 3 km freeway, 4 ramps, 4 regions); Kowloon, Hong Kong from OpenStreetMap (11 ramps, 18 perimeters) with TomTom OD demand; random demand with 30% standard deviation.

Ramp meters and perimeter gates affect each other, and training many RL agents together from scratch is unstable. In the authors' simulator, an asymmetric CTM moves vehicles along freeways and ramps, and a bathtub model with an MFD moves them inside urban regions. Early in training, an extra loss term makes each agent copy a classic controller: ALINEA for ramps, Gating for perimeters. The weight of this copy term fades to zero, so the agent can later find better actions than its teacher. Idea to remember: classic traffic controllers can act as teachers that get RL started.

An agency already running ALINEA or MFD-based gating could use those controllers as teachers to train a coordinated network controller in a calibrated simulator before any field test.

P-GASR2024

Physics-guided Active Sample Reweighting for Urban Flow Prediction

Jiang et al. · CIKM 2024 · paper ↗ · also 2a Physics-shaped layers

Traffic task
Predict next-step inflow and outflow of bikes or taxi passengers for every grid cell of a city, at 30-minute or 1-hour intervals.
Physics used
A continuity (conservation) equation on the grid graph, discretized in time: change in a cell's latent density = learned inflow term − learned outflow term.
AI model
Spatio-temporal graph blocks learn a latent density per cell; a graph convolution (ChebNet) gives the flux terms; an MLP turns density into flows; dropout runs measure uncertainty.
Where the physics enters
Architecture: z(T+1) = z(T) + σ(g(A, inflow)) − σ(g(A, outflow)). Data: each training sample is weighted by its conservation consistency plus model uncertainty, then the network is retrained.
Data
NYCBike1, NYCBike2, NYCTaxi and BJTaxi grid datasets, split 7:1:2; a robustness test replaces 10%, 30% or 50% of samples with Gaussian noise.
Key linesample weight ε_i = α·u_i + β·c_i, with u_i = spread of predictions over dropout runs and c_i = ‖ŷ(T+1, i) − (A·x)(T, i)‖⁻²

Real flow records often break conservation because of sensor errors or coarse time steps, and such samples can mislead a physics-guided model. The authors build a network shaped like a discretized continuity equation: next latent density = current density + learned inflow − learned outflow over the grid graph. Pre-trained copies then score each held-out sample on two things: how unsure the model is (spread of predictions with dropout left on), and how close a cell's predicted flow is to the flow arriving from its neighbours. The model is retrained with these scores as sample weights. Idea to remember: physics can decide which data to trust, not only shape the model.

What they found
  • NYCTaxi inflow MAE (Table 2): 12.05 for the physics-shaped network with equal sample weights versus 11.92 with physics-guided reweighting; ST-SSL, which uses the same spatio-temporal blocks without physics, had 12.37.
  • Noise test (Fig. 3): as more training samples were replaced with Gaussian noise, the equal-weight physics network got worse, while P-GASR deteriorated less.
For mobility

A transit or ride-hail operator could down-weight records that break flow conservation, such as faulty counts, when training demand forecasts, instead of cleaning the data by hand.

Watch out

The conservation check is loose (a cell's predicted flow versus its neighbours' earlier flows, not a vehicle balance), and gains over the equal-weight physics network are small.

Traffic task
Rebuild the full space-time density on a 1 km road (ring road or signalized arterial) from initial densities, boundary sensors or sparse probe-vehicle trajectories.
Physics used
LWR with a concave fundamental diagram (free-flow speed 60 km/h, jam density 120 veh/km, capacity 1800 veh/h), solved with the Godunov scheme to make reference solutions.
AI model
A Fourier neural operator: layers that mix information through frequency components and map a whole input grid to a whole density grid in one pass.
Where the physics enters
Data: Godunov LWR solutions from random step and pulse inputs are the training labels. Loss: a cell-by-cell conservation check on the predicted density is added (π-FNO).
Data
Over 12,000 simulated LWR solutions; trained on up to 3 queues and 2 signal cycles, tested on up to 40 queues and 8 cycles; one fine-tuned check on pNeuma (Athens) trajectories.
Key lineloss = (‖û − u‖/‖u‖)² + λ·R², R = Σ over cells |û(x, t+Δt) − û(x, t) − (Δt/Δx)·(q̂ in − q̂ out)|

This paper trains a Fourier neural operator (a network that maps a whole input grid to a whole output grid) to solve the LWR model. Traffic theory enters first through the data. The authors run a Godunov solver (the cell-based LWR scheme behind CTM) on random step-shaped initial densities (vehicle queues) and pulse-shaped boundary densities (signal cycles), because these inputs create the shocks and rarefactions seen on real roads. The network learns from these solutions. Second, a conservation check on every grid cell is added to the loss: density change must match inflow minus outflow. Idea to remember: pick simulated training inputs that produce the wave patterns you care about.

What they found
  • Ring-road initial-value problem (Table 1): test MAE was 1.298 veh/km with the conservation loss versus 2.579 veh/km for the same FNO trained on data alone; the gain was much smaller for the inverse problem.
  • Choice of training inputs (Fig. 23, boundary-value problem): with the proposed piecewise-constant inputs, test error grew with the number of initial queues roughly as x^0.45, versus x^0.75 for uniform-random and x^0.80 for Gaussian-process inputs.
For mobility

An agency could pre-train a fast density estimator on LWR simulations of its arterials, then fine-tune it on a few probe-trajectory samples, as the authors did with pNeuma.

Watch out

Training and most tests use simulated LWR solutions on 1 km roads; the real-data check is one fine-tuned pNeuma example, and the physics loss helped little for the inverse problem.

Mo & Di · UrbComp 2022 (KDD workshop) · paper ↗

Traffic task
Predict the distribution of a follower's next acceleration, not one value, from spacing, speed difference and speed, so that driver-to-driver randomness is captured.
Physics used
A stochastic IDM (its five parameters drawn from a Gaussian, plus output noise) or a stochastic Helly model; physics parameters are pre-trained, then learned jointly.
AI model
A conditional GAN: a generator maps (state, noise) to acceleration and a primal discriminator checks it against observed data; posterior estimators reduce mode collapse. Each network has 4 layers of 20 neurons.
Where the physics enters
Through a second (auxiliary) discriminator: at unlabeled states it tries to tell generator samples from stochastic-physics samples, and the generator learns to fool it; a mean/std matching term is added.
Data
Synthetic data from a stochastic IDM with normal or log-normal noise (500 labeled, 1,000 unlabeled states); NGSIM US-101 trajectories.

Earlier physics-informed GANs add a squared gap between the generator's acceleration and a single IDM value; the authors show this squeezes the predicted spread to zero (mode collapse). DoubleGAN treats the physics as random too: IDM parameters are drawn from a distribution, giving many plausible accelerations for each state. A second discriminator compares the generator's samples with these physics samples at unlabeled states, so the generator must match the whole physics distribution, not one number. A moment-matching term (compare means and standard deviations) speeds up early training. Idea to remember: when behavior is random, compare distributions with the physics, not single values.

  • Synthetic stochastic-IDM data, normal noise (Table 1): DoubleGAN reached RMSE 0.117 and KL divergence 0.543, the best RMSE and KL in the table, ahead of a plain GAN and of PhysGAN with a deterministic IDM loss.

For mobility

A simulation team could give each simulated driver realistic variability learned from data and a stochastic IDM, instead of one deterministic IDM driver.

Watch out

On NGSIM all models had similar RMSE (Fig. 7); the gain is mainly in the predicted spread (KL), and the best physics model must be found by trial.

Anisotropic CNN2022

Thonnam Thodi, Khan, Jabari & Menéndez · IEEE T-ITS 2022 · paper ↗ · also 1c Theory makes the data

Traffic task
Rebuild the full speed field of a freeway lane on a 10 m × 1 s grid from the trajectories of only a few probe vehicles (5% of traffic).
Physics used
Kinematic wave theory: speed changes travel forward at free-flow speeds (60–100 km/h) and backward in congestion at about 18 km/h. These three speeds fix the kernel shape.
AI model
An encoder–decoder CNN with six convolution layers turns an image of sparse probe trajectories on the space-time plane into the complete speed field.
Where the physics enters
In every convolution kernel: weights outside the two wave cones are reset to zero after each gradient step. Also in the data: the network is trained only on simulated traffic.

Training: Vissim microsimulation of an 800 m section of the E-22 Abu Dhabi–Al Ain road (free, slow and congested demand). Testing without retraining: NGSIM US-101 and HighD.

Probe-vehicle trajectories are drawn as an image on the space-time plane, and a CNN fills in the speed everywhere. An ordinary 7 × 7 kernel lets a cell borrow information from every direction, as if disturbances could travel at any speed. Kinematic wave theory says they cannot: in free flow they move downstream at about vehicle speed, in congestion upstream at about 18 km/h. So each kernel keeps weights only inside these two cones and zeros the rest after every training step. It is trained on Vissim runs only and tested on real NGSIM and HighD data. Design idea: let the physics decide which neighbours a convolution may look at.

What they found
  • Table 2 (simulated test data): the wave-cone CNN needs 215625 parameters versus 443193 for the ordinary CNN, a −51.4% change, with nearly the same average speed error.

For mobility

An agency with sparse probe or connected-vehicle data could rebuild detailed freeway speed maps, setting the kernel cones from the local free-flow speed range and congested wave speed.

Watch out

Average accuracy did not improve (Table 2); the gains are fewer parameters, less overfitting and cleaner shockwaves. Wave speeds are set by hand and must suit the site.

STDEN2022

STDEN: Towards Physics-Guided Neural Networks for Traffic Flow Prediction

Ji et al. · AAAI 2022 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Forecast the next hour of 5-minute traffic counts on every road segment of a city sub-network, using the past hour of counts.
Physics used
A continuity (conservation) equation for a hidden 'potential energy' at each junction. Flow on a road equals the potential drop between its two ends, like water running downhill.
AI model
A GRU encoder sets the starting potential at each junction. A neural ODE (a network used as dz/dt and stepped forward by an ODE solver) moves it ahead in time.
Where the physics enters
The ODE's right-hand side is the physics: ∂z/∂t = −ϕ ⊙ tanh(αΔz), a neighbour-difference (graph Laplacian) step with learnable node 'volumes' ϕ. Flows are then read off as potential drops.
Data
Beijing taxi GPS (about 40,000 taxis, April–July 2015) matched to roads; taxi counts per segment every 5 minutes on three sub-networks with 221, 393 and 564 segments.
Key line∂z/∂t = −ϕ ⊙ tanh(α Δz), and flow on road i→j: f_ij = −(z_i − z_j) (z = potential at junctions, Δ = graph Laplacian)

STDEN imagines a hidden 'potential energy' z at every road junction. Traffic runs from a road's higher end to its lower end, and the volume equals the drop: f = −(z_i − z_j). Putting this into a continuity equation gives a rule for how z changes: each junction is pulled toward its neighbours (graph Laplacian), scaled by a learnable node 'volume' ϕ. A GRU reads the past hour and sets the starting z. An ODE solver runs the rule forward one hour, and flows are read back as potential drops. Design idea: predict a hidden potential and derive flows from it, so the core step is a conservation-shaped equation.

What they found
  • Table 3: averaged over the three Beijing networks and the 15, 30 and 60-minute horizons, STDEN lowers MAE/RMSE/MAPE by 10.29%/13.49%/6.03% compared with the second-best method.
  • Ablation (Fig. 3, bar charts only): swapping the physics equation for a plain fully connected network (UnkP) gives higher errors; even an incomplete physics version without the node volume ϕ (IncP) beats it.
For mobility

A city could forecast link volumes and, from the same model, map a junction-level potential that shows where traffic is being pushed from and toward.

Watch out

The 'potential energy' is invented by the model, not measured; flow = potential drop is a diffusion-style analogy with no capacity or fundamental diagram, tested only on taxi counts.

AI model
Standard graph forecasters (GRNN, STGCN, DCRNN) with a 'Graph PDE layer' inserted before their graph-convolution steps.

Inside the layer: each node's state changes by upstream flux minus downstream flux on the sensor graph, plus H, with learnable rates and a weighted skip link to the old state.

GPDE starts from the ARZ model, assumes density stays fixed over the short forecast, and reduces it to an LWR-type equation for speed with a Greenshields flux. It then writes one explicit time step of this equation on the sensor graph (one-sided differences on a corridor, central ones at merges and diverges): a node's speed changes by the flux arriving from upstream minus the flux leaving downstream, plus a source term H for ramps. This step becomes a 'Graph PDE layer' with learnable rates and a weighted skip link, plugged into GRNN, STGCN or DCRNN. Design idea: one step of a numerical scheme can act as a message-passing layer.

Traffic task

Flow conservation at nodes: flow in minus flow out equals a known net injection c at each junction (B f = c, where B is the node–link incidence matrix).

A two-layer graph-attention network (GATv2) reads link features such as lanes, speed limit, road type and location, and weights 256 conservation-preserving moves; a least-squares step then fine-tunes.

In the output: the model starts from a balanced fill-in and may only add moves that keep every node balanced and every measured link unchanged. The last step allows a small, learned imbalance.
Data
LA County road graph (5,749 nodes, 7,498 links) with Caltrans PeMS 2018 daily counts on 2,879 links; also a European power grid and NYC Citi Bike.

FlowSymm sees the network as junctions (nodes) and links, with counts known on some links. Step 1: find the smallest fill-in for the missing links that makes flow in minus flow out match the known net injection at every node. Step 2: build 256 'circulation moves', patterns that shift flow around loops without changing any node balance or any measured link. Step 3: a graph-attention network reads link features and decides how much of each move to add. Step 4: a small least-squares step lets the result drift slightly from perfect balance to absorb sensor noise. Design idea: let the network choose only among moves that already respect conservation.

An agency with counts on only part of its links could fill in the rest so volumes balance at every junction, useful for network-wide daily volume maps.

Only static daily averages were tested (no time dynamics), net injections at nodes must be known, and sensors were hidden at random, not in real sensor layouts.

NFVM2026

Baba et al. · arXiv 2026 · paper ↗ · also 1a Equation in the loss

Traffic task
Solve the LWR model fast and accurately (density over time and space from initial and boundary densities), and reproduce real highway density waves.
Physics used
LWR conservation law ∂ρ/∂t + ∂f(ρ)/∂x = 0 with six flow–density shapes (Greenshields, two triangular, trapezoidal, Greenberg, Underwood), plus Burgers' equation.
AI model
A tiny fully connected network (about 1,200 to 1,800 weights) that outputs the flow across each cell boundary from nearby cell densities, and from past time steps in the larger version.
Where the physics enters
In the update rule: a cell's density changes only by boundary flow in minus flow out, so vehicles are conserved by construction. The unsupervised version is trained on the PDE's weak form.
Data
Synthetic: about 2,000 exact Riemann problems for training, 1,000 piecewise-constant tests with exact solutions. Real: Berkeley DeepDrive drone data, 400 m, four lanes, 15 minutes; trained on about 70 s.
Key lineρⱼ(n+1) = ρⱼ(n) + (Δt/Δx) · [F_θ(ρⱼ₋₁, ρⱼ) − F_θ(ρⱼ, ρⱼ₊₁)], where F_θ is a small neural network (result clipped to [0, ρ_max])

The paper keeps the finite-volume update used to solve LWR, the same bookkeeping as the cell transmission model: a cell's density changes by the flow entering across one boundary minus the flow leaving across the other. Only the boundary-flow formula, normally Godunov's, is replaced by a small neural network that looks at nearby cells. Because each boundary flow leaves one cell and enters the next, vehicles are conserved by construction. The network is trained on exact LWR solutions or, with no solutions at all, on the weak form (the equation checked in integrated form, which tolerates shocks). Design idea: learn only the uncertain piece and keep the conservation bookkeeping fixed.

  • Table 2 (symmetric triangular flux, L2 error): Godunov 2.2e−3, WENO 2.0e−3, basic NFVM 1.3e−3, larger NFVM (4 cells, 5 time steps) 2.9e−4, close to discontinuous Galerkin at 2.7e−4, which the paper says is far slower.

A traffic model as a layer

A real traffic model runs inside the pipeline. The network sets its parameters or inputs, and the training signal flows back through the model.

LESCMP2022

Learning the max pressure control for urban traffic networks considering the phase switching loss

Wang, Yin, Feng & Liu · Transportation Research Part C 2022 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Pick the signal phase at every time step for each of six intersections on Plymouth Rd., Ann Arbor, to reduce total stop delay, with no fixed cycle or phase order.
Physics used
Store-and-forward queue model plus a lost time at each phase switch. Switching-curve max pressure (SCMP) is proven throughput-optimal there: queues stay bounded whenever demand is within capacity.
AI model
PPO. The actor is the max-pressure controller itself, not a generic neural network; its parameters are cell weight curves (stopped and moving vehicles) and the switching curve F(x) = α·x^β. Critic: two-layer, 256-neuron network.
Where the physics enters
In the policy's structure. Pressure, phase choice and the switch-only-if-clearly-better rule come from the stability theory; the argmax becomes a softmax so PPO can explore and tune the curves.
Data
SUMO model of the six-intersection corridor (OpenStreetMap network, demand calibrated from evening-peak video); 60-minute episodes with five demand periods; extra tests at fixed relative demands from 0.2 to 1.2.
Key lineψ = max_s pr(x, s) − pr(x, s_now) − F(‖x‖); switch to the max-pressure phase only if ψ ≥ 0, with switching curve F(x) = α·x^β

Max pressure is a signal rule: at each step, give green to the phase whose movements have the most pressure, meaning upstream queue minus downstream queue, weighted by saturation flow and turning ratios. The classic rule ignores the time lost at each switch, so in heavy traffic it switches too often. The authors switch only when another phase beats the current one by F(total queue) and prove this keeps queues bounded in a store-and-forward network. For real traffic, pressure counts vehicles by position (cell weights), and PPO tunes those weights and F in SUMO. Idea to remember: theory fixes the policy's shape; RL only tunes its knobs.

What they found
  • Table 1 (same demand as training, 10 runs): mean system total delay was 331.98 h for max pressure without a switching curve (PWBP), 108.87 h with it (ESCMP) and 71.95 h after PPO tuning (LESCMP).
  • Fixed demand levels not used in training (Table 2): PPO tuning still helped, e.g., at relative demand 1.0 delay fell from 328.1 h (ESCMP) to 169.9 h (LESCMP).
For mobility

A city testing max pressure could keep its stability logic and let RL in a calibrated simulator tune the cell weights and switching margin for each intersection.

Watch out

One simulated corridor with every vehicle position known; SUMO's actuated control still had lower mean delay in Table 1 (68.56 vs 71.95 h) and at the highest Table 2 demand.

Son 20222022

Differentiable Hybrid Traffic Simulation

Son, Qiao, Sewall & Lin · ACM Trans. Graph. (SIGGRAPH Asia) 2022 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Learn green-time splits on a 4×4 grid of signals and a pace-car policy that holds a time-varying target speed; also recover initial traffic states from final states.
Physics used
ARZ second-order model solved with finite volumes (u_eq = u_max(1 − ρ^γ), γ = 0.5) on macroscopic lanes; IDM with randomized parameters on microscopic lanes; differentiable macro↔micro conversion.
AI model
A network of two fully connected layers (256 nodes each) outputs control inputs: signal times, or pace-car acceleration and steering. It is trained by gradient ascent on reward through the simulator.
Where the physics enters
The whole hybrid simulator sits after the network as a differentiable layer. Hand-derived gradients of the reward pass back through ARZ cells, IDM vehicles and lane conversions to each control input.
Data
Synthetic scenarios only: short lanes (three linked lanes in hybrid mode) for state recovery, a 4×4 signal grid with synthetic incoming-flow schedules, and a pace-car road; no field data.
Key lineARZ cell update Qᵢⁿ⁺¹ = Qᵢⁿ − (Δt/Δx)·[f(q_b) − f(q_a)]; its hand-derived derivatives ∂Qᵢⁿ⁺¹/∂Qⱼⁿ carry the reward gradient back to the network's control inputs

Most traffic simulators are black boxes: a learning agent can only try actions and watch the reward. This paper writes out every step of a hybrid simulator with its derivatives. Macroscopic lanes run the ARZ model in finite-volume cells, microscopic lanes run IDM vehicles, and at lane junctions cell flow is turned into discrete vehicles and vehicles are counted back into cell density, both in a differentiable way. A small network outputs signal timings or pace-car actions, the simulator runs, and the reward gradient flows back through the traffic equations to the network weights. Design idea: a differentiable simulator lets you train control with gradients instead of trial and error.

What they found
  • 4×4 signal grid in the hybrid simulator (Table 2): best reward 208.48 with simulator gradients versus 191.51 for SAC, 174.18 for DDPG and 158.18 for PPO, which treat the simulator as a black box.
  • Pace-car problem with IDM followers (Table 2): best reward 4482.87 with simulator gradients versus 3373.99 for SAC, 3218.19 for PPO and 4.97 for DDPG.
For mobility

A city could tune signal plans or connected-vehicle speed advice by gradient descent on a calibrated, differentiable simulator instead of slow trial-and-error reinforcement learning.

Watch out

All tests are small synthetic scenarios with no lane changing; the ARZ gradient can be unstable near shocks, and the method is untested on real data.

Tang 20242024

Physics-informed Machine Learning for Calibrating Macroscopic Traffic Flow Models

Tang, Jin & Ozbay · Transportation Science 2024 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Calibrate a CTM for each day's morning or evening peak on 6.2 km of I-210 East from loop flow and speed data, without solving a new optimization problem every day.
Physics used
Cell Transmission Model with on-ramp buffers and capacity drop; per-cell free-flow speed, nominal capacity, dropped capacity, jam density and congestion wave speed are calibrated.
AI model
Two LeNet-style networks. The encoder maps measurements plus boundary conditions to CTM parameters, squeezed by a sigmoid into preset bounds; the decoder maps parameters plus boundary conditions back to measurements.
Where the physics enters
The encoder's parameters are run through the real CTM. The loss pulls the decoder's output toward the CTM simulation and toward the measured data, so only sensible parameters lower it.
Data
PeMS 5-min flow and speed on I-210 East (Irwindale Ave. to Grand Ave.): 9 cells, 6 on-ramps, 4 off-ramps; 2017–2018 for training, 2019 for testing.
Key lineloss = Σ‖M̂ − M̃‖² + γ · Σ‖M − M̂‖², where M̂ = decoder output, M̃ = CTM run with the encoder's parameters, M = measurements (γ = 0.8)

Calibrating a CTM usually means solving a hard optimization problem per day, yet parameters such as capacity change from day to day. Here an encoder network reads one peak period of loop data plus the boundary conditions (demands, off-ramp ratios, downstream speed) and outputs CTM parameters for every cell. Those parameters go into the real CTM, which simulates the corridor, and into a decoder network that also predicts the measurements. Training makes the decoder copy the CTM and match the data, and the total error drops only when the encoder gives sensible CTM parameters. Design idea: make the hidden code of an autoencoder be the parameters of a traffic model.

What they found
  • Held-out test day, March 26, 2019 (Figs. 7–8): the CTM run with the encoder's parameters reproduced the observed congestion pattern in speed and density; this extended abstract gives no error numbers or baseline comparison.
For mobility

An agency could recalibrate a freeway CTM for every peak period with one network pass, and track day-to-day capacity changes, instead of rerunning an optimizer each day.

Watch out

This version is an extended abstract: one test day judged by eye, the missing-data variant not yet tested, and parameters assumed constant within each peak.

MPC-RL2025

Reinforcement Learning With Model Predictive Control for Highway Ramp Metering

Airaldi, De Schutter & Dabiri · IEEE T-ITS 2025 · paper ↗ · also 2d Steers at run time

Traffic task
Meter one on-ramp of a three-segment, two-lane highway (1 km per segment) to cut total time spent while keeping the ramp queue at 50 vehicles or fewer under random two-peak demand.
Physics used
Second-order METANET (density, speed, ramp queue; exponential equilibrium speed). Critical density ρcrit and exponent a are learnable and start 30% off their true values; free-flow speed is also 30% off.
AI model
No neural network. A parametric MPC with a 24-step horizon is the RL policy and Q-function; second-order LSTD Q-learning updates its 53 parameters from closed-loop data.
Where the physics enters
METANET is the MPC's prediction model, so every action comes from planning on it. Q-learning differentiates the MPC solution to tune METANET parameters and cost weights for control performance, not for fit.
Data
Simulation only: a three-segment benchmark highway with one mainstream origin and one metered on-ramp, random two-peak demands and downstream congestion; 80 four-hour training episodes, 15 random seeds.
Key lineθ ← θ − α·H⁻¹·p, with p = −Σ δᵢ·∇θQθ(sᵢ, aᵢ), where Qθ is the optimal cost of the METANET-based MPC and δ is the TD error

MPC for ramp metering is only as good as its METANET calibration; deep RL needs much data and handles queue limits poorly. Here the MPC itself is the RL policy. Every minute it predicts traffic 24 steps ahead with METANET and picks the ramp flow that minimizes total time spent, abrupt rate changes and queue violations. After each episode, Q-learning compares predicted and realized costs (the TD error) and adjusts METANET parameters and cost weights using gradients of the MPC solution. The model is tuned for control, not prediction, so ρcrit drifts away from its true value. Design idea: keep the traffic model inside the controller and let RL tune it.

What they found
  • Starting from a deliberately mis-set METANET model and untuned weights (Fig. 4): learning cut total time spent from around 1100 to 700 veh·h, while the same MPC without learning stayed at its poor start.
  • Against DDPG, a neural-network RL agent (Fig. 4): DDPG reduced control variability and queue violations much more slowly; it has 293 380 learnable parameters versus 53 for MPC-RL.
For mobility

A DOT could start from its existing METANET-based ramp-metering MPC and let it tune itself from closed-loop data, rather than recalibrating the model by hand.

Watch out

Tested only in METANET simulation on one three-segment network with one metered ramp; the learned METANET parameters drift from true values, so the model is no longer a calibrated predictor.

PeMTFLN2025

Knowledge-data fusion dominated vehicle platoon dynamics modeling and analysis: A physics-encoded deep learning approach

Lyu et al. · Information Fusion 2025 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Predict speed and gap of the six followers in a seven-vehicle platoon for the next 2 s, given the lead vehicle's future speed; also simulate whole platoons from their first 2 s.
Physics used
A linearized general car-following law: acceleration = gains × (speed error, gap error, relative speed), with signs f′v < 0, f′s > 0, f′Δv > 0, a sufficient condition for local stability.
AI model
PeMTFLN: a Mamba (state-space) block per vehicle, a variational encoder for driver randomness, causal attention across the platoon, and an attention decoder that outputs three gains per vehicle every 0.5 s.
Where the physics enters
In the last layer: a softplus with signs [−1, 1, 1] forces the gains to obey the stability signs, then a fixed car-following update gives acceleration, speed and gap. Training runs end-to-end through it.
Data
HIGH-SIM trajectories: 739 platoons of seven vehicles, 15 s each at 0.1 s steps, split 7:1:2 for training, validation and testing.
Key lineθ = [−1, 1, 1] · Softplus(decoder output); a(k) = θ(k) · (x(k) − x*), with x = (v, s, Δv) and x* = (mean past v, mean past s, 0)

Deep car-following models fit data but cannot be analysed; models like IDM can be analysed but are too rigid. PeMTFLN splits the work. Neural networks read about 2 s of each follower's history and the platoon's interactions, and output three time-varying gains: how strongly each driver reacts to speed error, gap error and relative speed. A softplus with fixed signs makes every gain meet the local-stability signs, and a fixed car-following update turns the gains into acceleration, speed and gap; the speed and gap errors train the whole chain. Design idea: let the network predict the parameters of a car-following law, not the trajectory itself.

What they found
  • Two-second platoon prediction on HIGH-SIM (Table 2): PeMTFLN had the lowest average errors, velocity RMSE 0.469 m/s and gap RMSE 0.643 m, though every compared network used the same physics block.
  • Platoon simulation against an IDM calibrated per vehicle by a genetic algorithm (Fig. 9): IDM drifted into overly cautious or aggressive driving, while PeMTFLN stayed close to the real trajectories.
For mobility

A simulation team could use these data-fitted yet interpretable driver gains in platoon or AV testing, and still run string-stability checks on the learned drivers.

Watch out

Every compared network uses the same physics block, so the gain over a pure neural network is not measured; the IDM comparison is visual, on three platoons.

WardropNet2025

WardropNet: Traffic Flow Predictions via Equilibrium-Augmented Learning

Jungel, Paccagnan, Parmentier & Schiffer · ICLR 2025 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Predict link flows on a road network for a new set of trips and road features, as a fast stand-in for an equilibrium simulator such as MATSim; one variant predicts flows per time step.
Physics used
Wardrop user equilibrium (no traveler can save time by switching route alone) with learned link latency functions; the best variant uses piecewise-constant latencies that jump at capacity thresholds.
AI model
A feedforward network, the same one used as the pure-ML baseline, maps link and node features (length, speed, capacity, lanes, nearby homes and workplaces) to latency parameters θ.
Where the physics enters
As the final layer: an equilibrium (flow) problem turns the predicted latencies into link flows. A Fenchel-Young loss with random perturbations gives a usable gradient through this combinatorial layer.
Data
Four stylized random networks (targets from a Wardrop solver or MATSim) and two Berlin district networks with MATSim flows; 9 training, 5 validation and 6 test instances per scenario.
Key lineθ = φ_w(x); ŷ(θ) = argmax over feasible flows y of [θᵀy − Ω(y)]; ∇θ loss = ŷ(θ) − ȳ (predicted minus observed flows)

A network that maps road features straight to link flows misses how trips pile onto the main roads that form shortest paths. WardropNet keeps route choice inside the model. A neural network reads each link's context and outputs the parameters of its travel-time (latency) function. An equilibrium layer then routes all trips with those latencies and returns link flows that conserve flow at every node. Because this layer is a combinatorial solver, plain backpropagation gives zero or undefined gradients; a perturbed Fenchel-Young loss fixes this, and its gradient is predicted minus observed flow. Design idea: let the network learn travel costs and let an equilibrium solver turn costs into flows.

What they found
  • Berlin district with MATSim flows (Fig. 3d): the piecewise-constant-latency pipeline (CL) cut the mean absolute error of the same network without the equilibrium layer (FNN) by 72%.
  • Time-variant square-world scenario (Fig. 3f): the CL pipeline beat the best pure-ML baseline, a graph neural network, by 23%.
For mobility

Planners could screen many demand, closure or pricing scenarios with fast learned link-flow predictions that still respect route choice, instead of running a full equilibrium simulation for each.

Watch out

Targets come from simulators (a Wardrop solver or MATSim), not field counts, with only 9 training instances per scenario; the simplest latency variant (ER) did poorly.

PERL2025

Physical enhanced residual learning (PERL) framework for vehicle trajectory prediction

Long et al. · Communications in Transportation Research 2025 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Predict a following car's acceleration, and from it its speed, 0.1 s or 5 s ahead, using 5 s of history of the follower and the three vehicles in front.
Physics used
Adapted Newell car-following model with one parameter, the wave speed w (4.01 m/s when calibrated on 12,000 samples): the follower repeats a leader's acceleration after a delay of gap ÷ w. IDM and FVD tested as alternatives.
AI model
A two-layer LSTM (a recurrent network for time series) that predicts only the residual: observed acceleration minus the Newell prediction. A GRU is tested as an alternative.
Where the physics enters
The calibrated Newell model makes the base prediction and defines the training target. The network learns only what Newell misses; final output = Newell acceleration + learned residual.
Data
NGSIM US-101: 20,000 samples of four-vehicle strings at 0.1 s; 300 to 12,000 training samples. This card follows the arXiv version; the journal version adds automated-vehicle data and other networks.
Key linea_PERL(t) = a_Newell(t) + r̂(t), with a_Newell(t) = a_leader(t − D/w); the LSTM r̂ is trained on r = a_observed − a_Newell

PERL predicts how a following driver will accelerate. Step one: an adapted Newell model with one parameter (the wave speed w) makes a physics guess: the follower copies a leader's acceleration after a delay set by the gap and w. Step two: an LSTM reads 5 s of history from four vehicles and learns only the error of that guess. The two are added. A PINN would put the physics in the loss as a penalty, which can pull the network toward a wrong model. Here the physics is the starting point and the network corrects it. Design idea: let physics carry the bulk and train AI on the leftover.

What they found
  • Main test with the Newell model (Figure 6A): PERL's edge is largest when training data are scarce; once training data exceed 1000 samples, its gap to the pure LSTM and the PINN becomes much smaller.
  • Sensitivity test with IDM as the physics part (Figure 8): PERL (LSTM+IDM) beats IDM alone, the pure LSTM and the PINN (LSTM+IDM) whenever the training set is smaller than 10000 samples.
For mobility

An AV team or agency can keep a calibrated car-following model and add a small learned correction, which helps most when only a few hundred trajectories are available.

Watch out

The gain fades as data grow, and a poorly calibrated physics model weakens PERL (FVD calibrated on little data did worse than IDM here).

Q-Net2025

Q-Net: Queue Length Estimation via Kalman-based Neural Networks

Gao et al. · arXiv 2025 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Estimate the queue length of a road section every 10 s at signalized intersections in Rotterdam, from loop-detector counts and aggregated floating-car speeds (aFCD: average probe speeds per road segment per minute).
Physics used
Vehicle conservation: the queue change comes from cumulative inflow minus outflow counts, corrected for unobserved exits. A two-regime model: the queued part runs at jam speed vj, the rest at free-flow speed vf.
AI model
A KalmanNet: a small GRU network (952 trainable parameters) that outputs the Kalman gain at each step, trained end to end on radar queue lengths.
Where the physics enters
The physics is the filter itself: conservation is the prediction model, the two-speed model is the measurement model. The network only sets the Kalman gain, the weight that decides how much a speed mismatch corrects the queue.
Data
16 days (6:00–20:00) on section N1-IN in Rotterdam: loop counts every 10 s, aFCD every 60 s, radar queues as ground truth; transfer tests on sections N3-IN and N3-OUT.
Key linex̂_t = (x̂_{t−1} + u_t) + K_t(θ) · (y_t − h(x̂_{t−1} + u_t)), where u_t is the queue change from loop-count conservation, h(·) the two-speed model and K_t(θ) the gain from a GRU

Q-Net keeps the Kalman filter loop. In the predict step, cumulative loop counts give the change in queue length: vehicles in minus vehicles out, a conservation balance, rescaled to metres and filtered. A two-speed model then turns the predicted queue into the speed each aFCD segment should show. In the update step, the gap between observed and expected speeds corrects the queue. A normal Kalman filter computes the correction weight (the Kalman gain) from assumed noise levels; here a small GRU network learns it from radar data. Design idea: keep the traffic model as the filter's skeleton and let AI decide only how much to trust each data source.

What they found
  • All-day error on section N1-IN (Table 3): Q-Net RMSE 86.77 m vs 87.81 m for XGBoost and 89.32 m for an LSTM using the same inputs. Averages are close; the paper's point is that the data-only models lag during fast queue changes (Figure 8d).
  • Ablation (Table 5): replacing the learned gain with a standard Extended Kalman Filter with preset noise (Q-EKF) raises all-day RMSE from 86.77 to 217.58; removing the loop-count queue change u_t raises it to 90.2.
For mobility

A city could estimate queues from existing loops and commercial probe speeds after a short radar campaign for training, then reuse the model on nearby sections.

Watch out

Tested on 16 days in one Rotterdam corridor; training needs radar ground truth, and on average errors Q-Net is only slightly better than XGBoost.

A linear feedback car-following controller a = Kd·Δd + Kv·Δv (Kd = 0.62, Kv = 0.37), where Δd is the spacing error under constant time headway (CTH). Human drivers in the simulation follow IDM.
AI model
A PPO reinforcement-learning policy (actor and critic networks) that outputs only a correction to the linear controller's acceleration.

Inside the policy: action = safety barrier(linear controller action + RL correction). The barrier, also physics based, projects any action that would push headway outside 1–3 s back into that range.

The sum then passes through a safety barrier that blocks actions that would push headway outside 1–3 s. All tests are simulations with IDM human drivers and fixed delays; in normal traffic PERPL beats pure RL only slightly, and the headway guarantee comes from the separate barrier.

CTG2023

Guided Conditional Diffusion for Controllable Traffic Simulation

Zhong et al. · ICRA 2023 · paper ↗ · also 2b Traffic model as a layer

Traffic task
Generate realistic trajectories for every vehicle in a scene for AV testing in simulation, while meeting rules chosen at test time: speed limit, target speed, goal waypoint, no collision, no off-road, stop sign.
Physics used
Vehicle kinematics, not traffic flow: a unicycle model turns acceleration and yaw rate into position, speed and heading. Traffic rules are written in signal temporal logic (STL), a formal language for rules over time.
AI model
A conditional diffusion model (U-Net of 1D temporal convolutions, with a ResNet encoder for map and history) that denoises over 100 steps to produce each vehicle's action sequence.

States are always computed from actions through the unicycle model, in training and sampling. At run time, the gradient of each STL rule's robustness score (how well the rule is met) shifts each denoising step.

When a user wants, say, a speed limit or no collisions, the rule is written in STL, which gives a differentiable score.   • Ablation (Table IV, speed-limit rule): with the unicycle dynamics turned off but guidance and filtration kept, realism deviation rises to 3.4204 and failure rate to 0.612, far above the full model in the table's first row; the paper says all metrics degrade.
For mobility

Simulation teams could build AV test scenarios, such as cut-ins, stop-sign compliance or slow traffic, by writing rules at test time instead of retraining a model.

Watch out

The physics is vehicle kinematics and traffic rules, not traffic flow; stronger guidance trades realism for rule satisfaction, and only vehicles in nuScenes were tested.

2d

Yu 20232023

Perimeter Control with Heterogeneous Metering Rates for Cordon Signals: A Physics-Regularized Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning Approach

Yu et al. · arXiv 2023 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Run the 20 signals on the cordon of a protected 5×5 grid so each gate meters inflow at its own rate, while the whole protected region stays near its best throughput.
Physics used
The protected region's MFD: total travel time (TTT) has a critical value, 17000 veh·s here, where network throughput peaks. The feedback is how far current TTT exceeds it.
AI model
One DDQN agent per cordon signal (a deep Q-network that scores each phase), trained only on local states: stopping time, leg occupancies, recent yellow phases and neighbors' actions.
Where the physics enters
Only at test time: when TTT exceeds the critical TTT, max((TTT − critical TTT)/Ks, 0), weighted by leg occupancies, is subtracted from the Q-values of non-perimeter phases before the phase is chosen.
Data
SUMO microsimulation: a 5×5 grid protected network with 20 gate links and two unbalanced, fluctuating demand patterns; agents trained on the north edge and reused at the other gates.
Key lineQ′(s, a) = Q(s, a) − (sum of relevant leg occupancies) × max((TTT − TTT_critical)/Ks, 0) for every phase a except the perimeter-control phase

Each cordon signal is an RL agent trained to cut local delay; it sees only its own intersection. The network-level physics is added afterwards. Every cycle (or every 5 s), the controller compares the protected region's total travel time with the critical value read from its MFD. If the region is over-full, the excess, divided by a weight Ks (750 here), is subtracted from the scores of all phases except the perimeter-control phase, which gives green only to traffic leaving the region. So gates close when the network needs it and local queues allow. Design idea: physics enters as a term in the action choice, with no retraining.

What they found
  • Ablation, demand 2 (Table 3): without the MFD term (MARL-local), total travel time inside the protected network is 96.22 vs 59.38 with it, and for the entire network 319.42 vs 233.18 (×10⁵ veh·s). Under demand 1, MARL-local gridlocked (Table 2).
  • Against the best classical perimeter controller, PI control (Tables 2 and 3): the physics-regularized MARL cuts total travel time of the entire network by 26.71% (demand 1) and 31.06% (demand 2).
For mobility

A city running adaptive or RL signals could add MFD-based perimeter protection by adjusting each controller's phase scores, without retraining the controllers for the whole network.

Watch out

Tested only in a simplified SUMO grid; the critical TTT must be read from the region's own MFD, and the weight Ks must be tuned for each network.

2d

Zhou 20242024

Enhancing System-Level Safety in Mixed-Autonomy Platoon via Safe Reinforcement Learning

Zhou, Yan & Yang · IEEE T-IV 2024 · paper ↗ · also 2c Physics first, AI corrects

Traffic task
Control the acceleration of one CAV, third in a five-vehicle single-lane platoon, so the platoon damps disturbances and keeps short headways while the CAV and the human cars behind it stay safe.
Physics used
Minimum time headway as the safe set: spacing s ≥ τ·v, τ = 0.3 s, written as control barrier functions. Human car-following: linear in spacing and speeds plus a learned bias; simulated humans follow OVM.
AI model
PPO actor-critic proposes the CAV's acceleration. A neural network learns the bias of each human driver's linear car-following model online. The barrier gains are trained with the actor through the QP layer.
Where the physics enters
At run time, a QP layer moves each PPO action to the nearest acceleration meeting the headway barrier constraints (hard for the CAV, softened for followers) and acceleration limits; in training, gradients pass through it.
Data
Simulation only: five-vehicle platoon, random head-vehicle speed noise, 500 training episodes. Tests: hard braking by a car ahead and a sudden acceleration by a human car behind the CAV.
Key lineu = u_RL + u_safe, with u_safe = argmin ‖u_safe‖² + Σσ² subject to ḣ + k·h + σ ≥ 0 for each safety margin h (CAV: h = s − τ·v, no σ)

PPO alone can learn smooth platoon control yet still crash. Here every PPO acceleration first passes a safety layer. A control barrier function is a safety margin h, here spacing minus τ times speed, plus a rule that h may shrink no faster than k·h, so it never drops below zero. The layer solves a tiny QP for the smallest change to the PPO action that obeys this rule for the CAV and, softly, for the human cars behind it, whose reactions come from an online-identified car-following model. Because the QP is differentiable, PPO learns with the filter in place. Idea to remember: RL proposes, headway physics vetoes.

What they found
  • Safety-region test (Fig. 5a): over a grid of braking strengths and durations by a car ahead, the set of collision-free cases was almost 60% larger with the safety layer than for PPO without it.
  • Sudden acceleration by the second human car behind the CAV, vehicle 4 (Fig. 11): pure car following, PPO without the safety layer, and the safety layer without car-following identification all collided; only the full method avoided collision.
For mobility

An AV developer or DOT testing cooperative cruise control could wrap a learned controller in a headway-based safety filter that also protects the human drivers behind the automated car.

Watch out

Simulation with one CAV and OVM humans; only the CAV's own headway is guaranteed (follower limits are softened), and the claimed capacity and string-stability gains are not quantified.

2d

PMA-Diffusion2026

PMA-Diffusion: A Physics-guided Mask-Aware Diffusion Framework for Traffic State Estimation from Sparse Observations

Liu, Jin & Choi · Transportation Research Part C 2026 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Fill in a full lane-level freeway speed field (200 cells of 100 ft, over 200 s) from loop detectors and a few probe vehicles, with as little as 5% of locations observed.
Physics used
Kinematic wave theory: speed patterns travel along a free-flow or a congested wave direction, as in Treiber–Helbing adaptive smoothing, plus a first-order transport residual ∂V/∂t + c ∂V/∂x ≈ 0.
AI model
A U-Net diffusion model (a generator that builds a sample by removing noise step by step) learns what speed fields look like; it is trained on masked, incomplete fields, so no full ground truth is needed.
Where the physics enters
Only at sampling. After each denoising step, observed cells are reset to the measurements; then the AAS projector smooths the unobserved cells along wave directions and reduces the transport residual. Training uses no physics.
Data
I-24 MOTION (Nashville) camera trajectories turned into speed fields; loop rows (5%, 15%, 25%) and probe trajectories are masked out of the full field to mimic sparse sensors.
Key lineR = (V_s,t − V_s,t−1) + c·(V_s,t − V_s−1,t), a discrete ∂V/∂t + c ∂V/∂x ≈ 0; unobserved cells are updated V ← V − α_char·R after the wave-direction smoothing

The paper treats traffic state estimation as filling in a speed image. First, a diffusion model learns what realistic I-24 speed fields look like, trained only on the cells that sensors actually see. To estimate a new field, the sampler starts from noise and denoises step by step. After each step it copies the measured cells back in. Then a physics projector changes only the missing cells: it blends smoothing along the free-flow and congested wave directions, chosen by local speed, and nudges cells to shrink a first-order transport residual. Design idea: physics as a plug-in step during sampling, which can be changed without retraining.

What they found
  • Table 2, prior trained on real sensor masks (single-mask), 5% detector rows, no probes: plain RePaint sampling becomes unstable (Masked-MSE 7.1959 on hidden cells); adding the physics projector (PMA) brings it to 0.0364.
  • Table 2, prior trained on full fields, same 5% setting: physics-only smoothing (AAS-only) gives Masked-MSE 0.1463, diffusion without physics (RePaint) 0.0172, and diffusion plus physics (PMA) 0.0167. Physics alone is weak; with a strong prior it adds little.
For mobility

An agency could train one speed-field model and reuse it as detector layouts and probe shares change, adding conservation or fundamental-diagram projectors if flow or density data exist.

Watch out

Tested only on I-24 MOTION with synthetic masks; the projector acts on speeds alone (no vehicle conservation), and its wave speeds and step sizes are fixed hyper-parameters.
