Huang 20232023

On the Limitations of Physics-Informed Deep Learning: Illustrations Using First-Order Hyperbolic Conservation Law-Based Traffic Flow Models

Huang & Agarwal · IEEE OJ-ITS 2023 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Rebuild the full density field ρ(x, t) from initial and boundary detector data (sometimes plus connected-vehicle samples), on a simulated ring road and on NGSIM US-101.
Physics used
LWR with a Greenshields fundamental diagram (hyperbolic, allows shocks) versus the same LWR plus a small diffusion term ε ∂²ρ/∂x² (parabolic, smooth); ε = 0.13 taken for NGSIM.
AI model
A standard physics-informed fully connected network maps (x, t) to density, trained (L-BFGS-B or Adam) on data error plus the PDE residual at 10,000 collocation points, where only the equation is checked.
Where the physics enters
Only as the test: the same network is trained with the hyperbolic LWR residual and with the diffusive one, then compared with a Lax-Friedrichs numerical solver; the PDE type explains the failures.
Data
Synthetic ring-road density generated from both PDE forms (240 × 960 grid); NGSIM US-101, 2,060 ft, 45 minutes, binned at 20 ft × 5 s.
Key lineloss = μ1 · data error + μ2 · mean[(∂ρ/∂t + vf(1 − 2ρ/ρm) ∂ρ/∂x − ε ∂²ρ/∂x²)²] at collocation points; ε = 0 is hyperbolic LWR, ε > 0 the parabolic version

The authors ask whether a physics-informed neural network can learn LWR when traffic has shocks. LWR is hyperbolic: its true solution jumps at a shock, so it has no smooth (strong) solution. They generate ring-road data with LWR and with LWR plus a small diffusion term, which makes it parabolic and rounds off the shock. The same network is trained with each residual and different mixes of boundary, initial and connected-vehicle data, then on NGSIM. It fits the smooth version but fails around the shock. Remember: what a residual loss can teach depends on the PDE type; shocks need diffusion, data near the shock, or a numerical solver.

What they found
  • Ring road, 10% of initial and boundary data, L-BFGS-B: relative L2 error 0.0164 with the diffusive (parabolic) residual versus 0.309 with the pure hyperbolic LWR residual (Table 1, Fig. 6).
  • NGSIM US-101 with only initial and boundary data: PIDL with the hyperbolic LWR has a relative L2 error of 0.345 and misses the shockwaves (Fig. 9); a classical Lax-Friedrichs solver with the same inputs does better and keeps them (Fig. 11).
For mobility

Before trusting a physics-informed estimator where stop-and-go waves occur, compare it with a numerical solver such as Lax-Friedrichs; consider a calibrated diffusion term or probe data near shocks.

Watch out

The ring-road data come from the PDEs used in the loss, and the field test uses only boundary and initial data; interior probe data helps a lot (authors' earlier work).

LASIL2024

LASIL: Learner-Aware Supervised Imitation Learning For Long-term Microscopic Traffic Simulation

Guo et al. · CVPR 2024 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Learn a microscopic city traffic simulator from drone trajectories that stays realistic over long closed-loop runs (800 s) in downtown Athens.
Physics used
Standard macroscopic traffic-flow quantities as the yardstick: road density (vehicles ÷ lane length) and road mean speed, compared with real data and a calibrated SUMO (IDM + MOBIL) baseline.
AI model
A graph-attention policy predicts each vehicle's next positions; a VAE blends the policy's own rollout states into the expert data so it learns to recover from drift; LQR smooths the trajectories.
Where the physics enters
Only at evaluation: after 800 s rollouts, each road's mean density and speed are compared with ground truth by RMSE and mapped. Training uses no traffic-flow equation.
Data
pNEUMA drone dataset (Athens): over half a million trajectories, about 100 km of lanes and 100 intersections; first 3 days for training, last day for testing.
Key lineroad density = vehicles on the road ÷ total lane length; macroscopic check = RMSE over roads between simulated and real density (and mean speed)

LASIL learns a city traffic simulator by imitating drone trajectories. Plain imitation (behavior cloning) drifts in long runs: small errors push vehicles into situations never seen in training, called covariate shift. LASIL uses a VAE that blends the learner's own rollout states into the expert data, so the policy learns to steer back toward real behavior. The traffic-flow part is the check: after 800 s of closed-loop simulation, the authors compute each road's mean density and speed and compare them with real data and with SUMO. Remember: a learned microsimulator should also pass a macroscopic test, not only short-term trajectory errors.

What they found
  • 800 s macroscopic check (Table 2): road density RMSE 45.13 veh/km and road speed RMSE 3.17 m/s for LASIL, versus 55.65 and 3.73 without the VAE augmentation.
  • On the same check, SUMO with calibrated IDM + MOBIL scores 52.70 veh/km and 5.52 m/s, and plain behavior cloning 61.51 veh/km with 42.15% of vehicles off-road (Table 2).
For mobility

An agency building a learned digital twin can use the same two-level test: short-term trajectory error plus long-run per-road density and speed against field data.

Watch out

The traffic-flow check is coarse: road-averaged density and speed RMSE in one city, with no fundamental-diagram, queue spillback or wave-speed test.

Sustained Heterogeneity2026

Sustained Heterogeneity: an emergent collective mechanism in LLM-driven traffic

Qi & Guan · arXiv 2026 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Check whether LLM agents acting as car-following controllers keep traffic stable: 22 cars on the 230 m Sugiyama ring, at four densities and different shares of LLM-driven cars.
Physics used
Sugiyama 2008 ring-road wave experiment; IDM (collision clamp and the non-LLM cars); traffic-theory controls: white and coloured noise, driver-parameter spread, IDM with delay, Optimal Velocity string instability.
AI model
GLM-4-Flash LLM with a Chinese prompt reads speed, gap and relative speed every 0.5 s and outputs a target-speed change plus a chain-of-thought explanation; a safety layer clamps unsafe commands.
Where the physics enters
Only as the test: the ring-road wave experiment, matched IDM and Optimal Velocity control runs, and a density versus LLM-share phase diagram judge the LLM fleet. Physics never trains the LLM.
Data
Simulation only: 170 runs of 300 s; 13,200 LLM decisions per full-LLM run (39,600 over three seeds); densities 43.5 to 95.7 veh/km.
Key linecritical LLM share p_c ∼ Δs_trigger(ρ) / (σ · τ_erosion · n), where Δs_trigger = spare gap beyond the IDM desired gap, σ = per-decision speed drift, τ_erosion = build-up time, n = number of cars

The authors put 22 LLM-driven cars on the 230 m ring of the famous Sugiyama experiment. Every 0.5 s each LLM picks a target-speed change; an IDM-based layer only blocks collisions. The LLM fleet forms stop-and-go waves, while an all-IDM fleet stays smooth. To find out why, they run the classic traffic-theory explanations as matched controls (random noise, driver differences, reaction delay, Optimal Velocity instability); none makes waves of similar size. They then map the LLM share that triggers waves at each density. Remember: a ring-road wave test across densities and penetration rates can expose collective instability that each agent's sensible reasoning hides.

What they found
  • In matched control runs, driver-parameter spread and IDM with an input delay give a velocity standard deviation below 0.001 m/s, versus 2.12 m/s for the all-LLM fleet (Sec. 4.1, Table 3).
  • At the highest density, stop-and-go appears once the LLM share passes a threshold between p = 0.18 and p = 0.27 (Sec. 4.3, Fig. 3a); on the sparsest ring even an all-LLM fleet stays in free flow.
For mobility

Before LLM-based controllers drive in mixed traffic, run them through a Sugiyama-style ring test across densities and penetration rates, and enforce stability in the low-level controller.

Watch out

Simulation only, with one LLM (GLM-4-Flash), one Chinese prompt and hand-tuned safety-layer thresholds; the authors say the absolute p_c values are model-specific.

Lane 20242024

Validating a data-driven framework for vehicular traffic modeling

Lane & Roy · J. Phys.: Complexity 2024 · paper ↗

Traffic task
From trajectories alone, find which neighbors a car reacts to and write its acceleration equation; tested on single-lane ring-road data where the true car-following model is known.
Physics used
IDM and the Optimal Velocity Model generate the data (314 m ring, 30 cars jammed, 15 free); their equations, rewritten as polynomials, give the true terms the method must recover.
AI model
Step 1: transfer entropy and its conditional version (how much a neighbor's past improves prediction of my next move). Step 2: SINDy-PI sparse regression keeps a few terms from a 250-term polynomial library.
Where the physics enters
Known car-following models make test data with a known answer; their terms are mixed with redundant terms in the candidate library. Success means keeping the true terms, right coefficients, and no extras.
Data
Synthetic only: IDM and OVM ring-road runs at 0.1 s; 29 000 samples per vehicle for the information step; 4,000 training and 2,000 test points for SINDy-PI; Gaussian noise added later.
Key lineẊ ≈ Θ(X) Ξ with most entries of Ξ zero (SINDy); SINDy-PI uses the implicit form Θ(X, Ẋ) ξ = 0, with the leader's position and speed as inputs

The paper tests a two-step recipe for discovering a car-following law, using simulated cars whose true law is known. First, information measures check which vehicle influences a subject car: the leader, the car two ahead, or the follower. Conditional transfer entropy, which removes indirect effects, correctly points to the leader only. Second, SINDy-PI (sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics) builds the acceleration equation from a few terms of a large polynomial library. It recovers the IDM and OVM terms on clean data, but success drops sharply once small measurement noise is added. Remember: validate a discovery tool on a known traffic model before trusting it on real trajectories.

What they found
  • Jammed OVM traffic: conditional transfer entropy from the leader averages 0.5120 nats versus 0.0109 nats from the follower, so only the leader matters (Fig. 2d).
  • On clean IDM data with library Θ3, SINDy-PI kept all true terms and no extra ones (100% specificity and accuracy); with library Θ5 it let in extra terms, falling to 64.1% specificity and 70.42% accuracy (Table 3).
For mobility

Before fitting a car-following law to drone or probe trajectories, an analyst can first test who influences whom (for example, multi-leader effects) and then get a short, readable equation.

Watch out

Tested only on simulated data with the true terms placed in the library; SINDy-PI fails once added noise exceeds about 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁴ (Fig. 3), so real data remain untested.

TR-Agent2025

Automating Traffic Model Enhancement with AI Research Agent

Guo et al. · Transportation Research Part C 2025 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Improve three classic models automatically: IDM car-following (spacing error), MOBIL lane-change decisions (F1 score), and the LWR speed–density relation (speed error by density regime).
Physics used
IDM, MOBIL, and the Greenshields line v = vf(1 − ρ/ρm) used with LWR; each is the starting equation the agent edits and the baseline it must beat.
AI model
A GPT-4 agent with four modules: Idea Generator (with literature retrieval), Code Generator (writes and debugs Python), Evaluator (fixed scripts on real data), Analyzer (explains failures, suggests the next edit).
Where the physics enters
The classical equation is the seed: the LLM proposes interpretable structural edits and iterates until the error beats the original by a set threshold. No neural network is trained.
Data
Shanghai expressway car-following events (7,960), NGSIM I-80 lane changes, PeMS08 detectors; further tests on Lyft, NGSIM, SPMD, Waymo, HighD, PeMS04 and five urban datasets.
Key lineLWR speed–density: v = vf(1 − ρ/ρm) → v = vf(1 − L), with L = 1 / (1 + e^(−k(ρ − 0.5ρm)))

TR-Agent turns model improvement into a loop run by an LLM. It reads papers, proposes a change to a classic traffic equation, writes the code, runs it on real data, reads the error report, and tries again until the error drops past a set target. On LWR, it replaced the straight Greenshields speed–density line with an S-shaped (logistic) curve that lowers speed smoothly toward jam density. On IDM, it blended free-road and interaction terms with a smooth switch and softened hard braking. Each step leaves a written reason. Remember: an LLM can search equations fast, but you must judge whether each edit is physics or curve fitting.

What they found
  • LWR speed–density tested on unseen PeMS04 data: average speed MAE 4.60 for the original linear relation versus 2.76 for the agent's logistic version (Table 3).
  • Refined IDM on a dataset it was not built on: spacing MAE on Lyft falls from 45.61 m to 28.22 m (Table 1).
For mobility

A modeling team could let an agent like this screen many candidate edits to a car-following or speed–density model, then review the logged reasons before adopting any.

Watch out

Edits are empirical fits, not derivations (authors say so for LWR), and the classical FVD model still beats the refined IDM on spacing error on all six test sets (Table 1).

TRAFFIC-PDE-LEARN2025

Neural Networks Enabled Discovery On the Higher-Order Nonlinear Partial Differential Equation of Traffic Dynamics

Wei, Zhang, Liu & Zhou · arXiv 2025 · paper ↗

Traffic task
Find the equation for how occupancy changes over time on a 32-mile freeway section from sparse, noisy detector data, then use it to forecast flow 3 to 15 minutes ahead.
Physics used
General PDE form ∂t o = F(o, q, v and their first and second space derivatives); flow and speed tied to occupancy by fundamental diagrams that can vary along the road; CTM as benchmark.
AI model
Three neural networks with rational activations rebuild smooth occupancy, flow and speed; automatic differentiation gives exact derivatives; sparse regression with an L1 penalty and thresholding picks polynomial terms.
Where the physics enters
In the structure and the loss: flow and speed networks take rebuilt occupancy as input (a learned, location-varying FD), and a PDE loss forces ∂t o to equal a short sum of candidate terms.
Data
Caltrans PeMS, I-5 northbound, Kern County, Aug 15 2023, 06:00–18:00; 3-minute steps, 2-mile cells, detectors at 10 of 17 locations.
Key line∂t ô = Θ(ô, q̂, v̂, ∂x ô, ∂x q̂, ∂x v̂, ∂x² ô, ∂x² q̂, ∂x² v̂)ᵀ ξ; loss = data error + η_PDE · mean[(∂t ô − Θᵀξ)²] + η_spar · ‖ξ‖₁

Instead of assuming LWR or ARZ, TRAFFIC-PDE-LEARN lets loop-detector data choose the equation. Step 1: neural networks turn sparse, noisy data into smooth fields of occupancy, flow and speed; flow and speed are learned as functions of occupancy plus location and time, a fundamental diagram that can change along the road. Step 2: automatic differentiation gives derivatives of these smooth fields, avoiding noisy finite differences. Step 3: sparse regression keeps a few terms from a library of products of the variables and their derivatives. On I-5 the result is a second-order nonlinear PDE that forecasts flow better than CTM. Remember: smooth with a network, then differentiate, then pick terms.

What they found
  • Flow forecasts from the discovered higher-order PDE: RMSE 1.58 veh/3-min at 3 minutes ahead and 7.32 at 15 minutes, the lowest of the five models in Table II.
  • The classical CTM on the same corridor: RMSE 5.57 at 3 minutes and 10.00 at 15 minutes (Table II); LSTM and RNN do worse than CTM.
For mobility

An agency with loop data on a corridor could test whether LWR or CTM is enough there, or whether higher-order terms are needed, before picking a simulation model.

Watch out

One freeway section and one day; the discovered PDE has many small terms that are hard to read physically, and results depend on tuned loss weights and thresholds.

Group 1 makes a property likely. Only a property built into the model (2a, 2b) or forced on each output as it is made (2d) holds every time. 2aYesThe built-in property, for every output: vehicles conserved cell by cell (NFVM), each output reads only inputs inside the allowed wave cones (anisotropic CNN). Often with fewer parameters: 51.4% fewer for the wave-cone CNN.Harder to design, and only the built-in property is guaranteed. Clipping densities can break exact conservation (NFVM), and FlowSymm’s last step allows a small imbalance on purpose.STDEN, anisotropic CNN, GPDE, NFVM, FlowSymm
2bYesThe output is a traffic-model output, so it obeys that model, and the parameters keep their meaning. MPC-RL learns 53 parameters; the neural RL agent it was compared with has 293 380.The model runs in every pass and must pass gradients back. If it is wrong for the site, the network cannot fix it, and tuned parameters can drift from true values (MPC-RL).LESCMP, Son 2022, Tang 2024, MPC-RL, WardropNet, PeMTFLN
2cYesA sensible answer even when the learned correction is poor, and good results from little data: PERL’s edge was largest below about 1000 training samples.The gain fades as data grow. The correction can still break the physics unless something stops it: PERPL’s headway guarantee comes from a separate safety barrier.PERL, PERPL, Q-Net
2dYesEach output is pushed toward the rule as it is made. In CTG, speed-limit violations fell from 1.380 to 0.019. A safety layer that projects every action onto a hard headway constraint keeps that headway each time (Zhou 2024).Slower sampling or planning, and hand-set step sizes. Strong steering can pull outputs away from realistic traffic, and a constraint that is only softened is not guaranteed: Zhou 2024 protects the automated car’s own headway, not the followers’.CTG, PMA-Diffusion, Yu 2023, Zhou 2024
3–A clear answer on whether a model breaks a piece of traffic theory.A test covers only what it measures: LASIL’s road-average density check has no wave-speed or spillback test.Huang 2023, LASIL, Qi & Guan
4–Candidate equations for an engineer to judge.Found terms can fit noise. SINDy-PI failed once added noise passed about 10⁻⁶ to 10⁻⁴; TR-Agent’s edits are fits, not derivations.Lane & Roy, TRAFFIC-PDE-LEARN, TR-Agent

Choosing a way in

  1. Name what must never break. If a property must hold for every output (vehicles conserved, headway within limits, flows at equilibrium), build it into the model or project every output onto it: 2a, 2b or 2d.
  2. Ask how much you trust the theory at this site. A model you trust roughly belongs in the loss (1a, 1b) or as a starting point that a network corrects (2c). A hard layer cannot repair a wrong model.
  3. Count your data. Physics buys the most with few detectors or a few hundred trajectories. With more data, the gains shrink (PIDL-CF, PERL), and at 25 or 50 detectors a plain meta-trained network beat MAML-MTPINN.
  4. Test with traffic theory either way (3), against a classical baseline the paper can be beaten by: adaptive smoothing, a calibrated IDM, a Lax-Friedrichs or Godunov solver, MPC.

How the field moved

2021: the residual in the loss is the default. Networks learn car-following (PIDL-CF) and freeway density (PIDL+FDL) with an IDM or LWR error added to the loss; a Gaussian process is regularized the same way (PRGP). RL learns perimeter control inside an MFD simulator (MFDRLPC).

2022: generative models take up the residual (TrafficFlowGAN), and a discriminator learns to judge against a stochastic car-following model (DoubleGAN). Physics moves into the layers: wave cones in CNN kernels, a diffusion-like ODE on a road graph (STDEN). A whole traffic simulator becomes a differentiable layer (Son 2022). Max-pressure theory enters signal-control RL three ways: as the reward (Ma 2022), as the state the agent sees (Advanced-MP), and as the structure of the agent itself (LESCMP).

2023: the limits get named. A pure hyperbolic LWR residual cannot hold a shock (Huang 2023). Traffic rules start steering samples at run time (CTG), and an MFD term corrects an RL agent’s choices as it acts (Yu 2023).

2024: theory makes and weighs the data: designed LWR training inputs (π-FNO), conservation-based sample weights (P-GASR), ALINEA and Gating as teachers (Hu & Ma). A CTM becomes a calibration layer (Tang 2024). Traffic theory starts testing other AI: macroscopic checks of a learned microsimulator (LASIL), and of equation discovery itself (Lane & Roy).

2025–2026: hybrids that keep the traffic model in charge (PERL, PERPL, Q-Net, MPC-RL), equilibrium and conservation built into the output (WardropNet, NFVM, FlowSymm), and physics at sampling time for diffusion models (PMA-Diffusion). Safe RL for automated platoons and lane changes adds a safety layer that projects every action onto a barrier-function constraint built from a time-headway gap (Zhou 2024 and 2026, Yang 2025, Hegde 2025). LLMs arrive on three sides: as a teacher whose labels are checked for string stability (KIDL), as drivers tested on the Sugiyama ring (Qi & Guan), and as a research agent that edits IDM and LWR (TR-Agent).

Check yourself

1. A district has a radar detector every 2 miles on 10 miles of freeway and wants a speed map every minute. Which section do you start from, and what would make you switch?

Few detectors is where physics pays most, so start in 1a (PIDL+FDL, PRGP) or, if you already have a generative prior, a run-time projection (2d, PMA-Diffusion). Check the shocks first: a pure hyperbolic LWR residual misses them (Huang 2023), so add a diffusion term, interior probe data, or use a model whose layers respect the wave speeds (2a, the wave-cone CNN). Switch to a CTM layer (2b) if the map must obey a calibrated model exactly or you also need its parameters. Compare everything with adaptive smoothing.

2. A vendor offers a “physics-informed” learned car-following model for your microsimulator. Which two questions place it on the map, and what do you test before using it?

Where does the physics enter, and is it still there when the model runs? If it was only in the loss (1a, 1b), nothing stops a wrong-signed response in a state it never saw. Test it the way the section 3 papers do: the RACER sign check of how acceleration responds to speed, gap and closing speed; KIDL’s string-stability test at equilibrium; a Sugiyama ring at several densities (Qi & Guan). Compare it with a calibrated IDM on the same data.

3. A generated density field must conserve vehicles exactly, because it feeds a capacity analysis. Which sections can promise that, and which only make it likely?

A finite-volume update in the layers (2a, NFVM; watch the clipping), a CTM run that produces the output (2b), or a run-time projection onto conservation (2d). Note that PMA-Diffusion’s projector works on speeds and does not conserve vehicles, and FlowSymm relaxes the balance on purpose in its last step. Everything in group 1 makes conservation likely, on average.

4. An RL perimeter controller was trained in a two-region MFD simulator. What worries you before a city pilot, and what would you add?

It is 1c: the agent learned the simulator. In Zhou & Gayah, MPC beat the agents at most MFD-error levels, and when the true MFD was much higher than assumed both did worse than no control. Test across MFD errors, and keep theory at run time: an MFD correction on the agent’s choices (Yu 2023), default actions from control theory (Zhou 2023, listed under 2d), or a model-based controller that the agent only corrects (2c).

5. A city wants RL to run a corridor’s signals, and the operations manager asks what keeps it from doing something unstable. Which design do you show, and what is the honest caveat?

Show a design where theory fixes the controller’s shape. In LESCMP (2b) the agent is a max-pressure controller with a switching curve, a structure proven to keep queues bounded in a store-and-forward network; RL only tunes its cell weights and switching margin. A theory-based reward (1b, Ma 2022) or state (1c, Advanced-MP) shapes training but leaves the trained network free. The caveat: the proof is for an idealized network, and in the paper’s own SUMO test, actuated control still had a slightly lower mean delay (68.56 h against 71.95 h). Compare against your current actuated plans before any claim.
